title.en: Practice: Interpersonal skills: situations at work and dealing with the public
title.hi: अभ्यास: अंतर-वैयक्तिक कौशल: काम की स्थितियाँ और जनता से व्यवहार

section: Practice (written by us, not from a UPSC paper): Interpersonal skills: situations at work and dealing with the public

en.stem: Your senior proposes a plan at a meeting that you believe will fail for a reason the senior may not know. What should you do?
options: Say nothing and let it fail
Tell colleagues afterwards that the plan is poor
Give the reason to the senior courteously, with an alternative, before the plan is finalised
Write to the senior's superior
en.why: Disagreement is given to the senior directly, with reasons and an alternative, before the decision. Silence and talk behind the back both fail the matter.

en.stem: A colleague of your rank regularly sends you data late, which delays your reports. What do you do first?
options: Speak to the colleague directly, explain the effect, and agree on a date for the data
Complain to your common senior
Send your own reports late in return
Mention it to other colleagues
en.why: A peer's lapse is raised with the peer first. The senior comes in only if that fails.

en.stem: A clerk under you has made an error in a letter that has gone out. A visitor points it out in front of other staff. What is the best response?
options: Scold the clerk in front of the visitor
Deny that there is an error
Tell the visitor the clerk is new
Thank the visitor, say the office will correct it, and speak to the clerk privately afterwards
en.why: Before outsiders the head takes responsibility for the team's work; the correction is made in private.

en.stem: An elderly man who cannot read asks at your counter how to fill in a pension form. The queue is long. What should you do?
options: Tell him to bring someone who can read
Arrange for a staff member or the help desk to fill in the form with him, and keep the queue moving
Ask the person behind him to help
Tell him the form is self-explanatory
en.why: Where a person cannot manage the procedure, the office helps with it. The second option does so without being unfair to those waiting.

en.stem: A visitor shouts at you about a delay that was caused by another section. What is the best first response?
options: 'This is not my section's fault.'
'Lower your voice or leave.'
Let him finish, acknowledge the delay, and find out from the other section where the matter stands
Walk away until he is calm
en.why: To the visitor the office is one. Hearing him out and acting on the delay deals with both the person and the matter.

en.stem: Two members of your team both want the same week of leave, and only one can be spared. What is the best approach?
options: Find out from each why that week matters, and look for an arrangement that meets both needs, such as splitting the week or shifting one by a few days
Give it to the one who asked first, without discussion
Refuse both
Let them settle it between themselves
en.why: Asking why each wants the week may show that both needs can be met. That is working the conflict out together.

en.stem: You realise that a wrong figure in your note led your senior to give a wrong reply to a query yesterday. What should you do?
options: Hope that no one notices
Correct your own file quietly
Blame the clerk who typed the note
Tell the senior at once, give the correct figure, and offer to draft the correction
en.why: Bad news goes up early, with the remedy. A prompt and specific admission lets the senior correct the reply.

en.stem: A member of your team has done an excellent piece of work on a difficult file. What is the best way to recognise it?
options: Say nothing; it is the member's job
Mention the work and the person by name at the team meeting and tell your senior
Present the work to your senior as the team's, without naming anyone
Give the member less work next month
en.why: Praise is given in public and credit goes to the person who earned it.

en.stem: A group of thirty residents arrives at your office, all speaking at once about a broken drain. What should you do?
options: Refuse to meet a crowd
Promise that the drain will be repaired by evening
Ask them to choose a few people to speak, hear them, say what you can do and by when, and keep to it
Tell them to submit a written application and leave
en.why: A few speakers make hearing possible; a clear and honest commitment with a date deals with the matter. A promise that may not be kept makes things worse.

en.stem: A well-dressed visitor asks to be attended to ahead of the queue because he is 'known to the minister'. What do you say?
options: Attend to him first to avoid trouble
Tell him courteously that everyone is attended to in turn, and that his turn will come
Tell him loudly that such talk will not work here
Send him to your senior
en.why: Like cases are treated alike. The refusal is firm on the matter and courteous to the person; a loud rebuke is neither needed nor fair.

en.stem: Which way of handling a conflict is described here: 'Each side gives up a part of what it wanted so that the matter can be closed'?
options: Compromise
Avoiding
Forcing
Giving in
en.why: In a compromise each side gets a part. In giving in, one side yields entirely; in forcing, one side prevails; in avoiding, nothing is settled.

en.stem: A new junior is hesitant to ask questions and makes avoidable errors. What should you do?
options: Wait for the junior to learn from the errors
Point out each error in front of the team
Report to your senior that the junior is unsuitable
Meet the junior privately, go through the work, say that questions are welcome, and set a regular time for them
en.why: Correction is private, specific and joined to a way of doing better. Making questions welcome removes the cause.

en.stem: Your senior has taken a lawful decision after hearing your objection, and has not accepted your view. What should you do?
options: Carry it out slowly
Tell your team that you disagree with it
Carry out the decision fully
Ask for a transfer
en.why: Once a lawful decision is taken after a hearing, it is carried out in full. Undermining it before the team harms the work.

en.stem: A colleague begins telling you about the private faults of another colleague who is absent. What is the best response?
options: Listen and add what you know
Say, without rudeness, that you would rather not discuss someone who is not present, and turn to the work
Report the conversation to the absent colleague
Rebuke the speaker sharply
en.why: Declining plainly and politely respects both people. Joining in, carrying the tale and sharp rebuke each damage a working relation.

en.stem: A citizen's application is incomplete: two documents are missing and one signature is needed. How should the counter staff tell her?
options: Give her a written list of all three things, explain each, and say when she can come back
Tell her the application is incomplete
Tell her about the first missing document now and the rest when she returns
Return the application without comment
en.why: Everything that is needed is told at once and clearly, so that she does not have to return more than once.
